articles.title: Not used since the Korean War; US Army practices digging mass battlefield graves, 'If we went to war tomorrow...'
articles.summary: The US Army conducted a rare test practice of digging mass battlefield graves that have not been needed since the Korean War.
articles.body: The US Army conducted a rare test practice of digging mass battlefield graves that have not been needed since the Korean War. The Army reported that soldiers in North Carolina completed a “test-of-concept” exercise for large-scale battlefield temporary interment. Soldiers with the 3rd Corps Sustainment Command and the 20th Engineer Brigade, based in Fort Bragg, North Carolina, as well as religious support personnel like military chaplains, used diggers and excavators to see how effectively they could be used to help preserve bodies intact until they could be identified and repatriated to the US.“This exercise allowed us to take a critical look at how we respect, honor, and systematically manage our fallen in a high-intensity conflict,” said Sgt. 1st Class Delbert Ruede, the senior fatality management NCO for the 3rd CSC, in a statement. "If we went to war tomorrow, we would be making this up as we went along. What we are doing here is taking a scientific, field-tested approach so that we can maintain positive control and respectfully care for our fallen.”The core of the exercise, conducted near the St. Mere Eglise Drop Zone, evaluated whether heavy earthmoving equipment could excavate and backfill temporary plots rapidly without causing structural collapse or damage to remains.In theory, a standard temporary interment plot consists of five parallel trenches designed to hold 100 casualties -- ten laid on each side of a trench. In previous exploratory trials, units attempted excavation using standard backhoes, averaging three hours per trench for only ten remains. During Dragon Covenant, operators from the 27th Engineer Battalion, 20th Engineer Brigade, utilized D6 bulldozers, completing a full 20-remains trench in an average time of one hour and 15 minutes. During the dig, the team realized they needed to adjust from published spatial standards. Doctrine originally called for a seven-foot corridor between rows, which proved two feet too narrow for a dozer's tracks to navigate without disturbing the burial area.“We realized quickly that the existing measurements in the book didn’t accommodate the physical reality of the equipment,” Sgt 1st Class Delbert Ruede, the senior fatality management NCO for the 3rd CSC, said. “To prevent running over the remains, we expanded the trench to a 15-foot width and maintained a nine-foot pillar of undisturbed soil between each trench. That undisturbed pillar allows the dozer to drive along the center corridor and cast dirt inward to backfill without exerting direct downward pressure on the remains.”You use AI every day. articles.title: Iran targeted US air defenses then hit aircraft and buildings on Mideast bases, AP analysis finds
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — Iran's strikes on more than two dozen U. bases in the Middle East focused on early-warning systems before hitting aircraft and buildings, c...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Iran's strikes on more than two dozen U.S. bases in the Middle East focused on early-warning systems before hitting aircraft and buildings, causing billions of dollars in equipment damage , according to an Associated Press analysis.

The AP independently verified damage to American targets using satellite imagery from multiple providers and spoke to four regional officials who were briefed or have firsthand knowledge of what was hit. The AP found that, through August, more than 115 drone or missile strikes claimed by Iran or Iranian-backed militias damaged or destroyed structures on 26 military bases and other sites with U.S. equipment.

The AP found that Iran initially focused its attacks on aircraft hangars and systems that detect incoming strikes , clearing the way for further strikes on warehouses, troop housing and more.

The damage has significantly reshaped the American foothold in the Middle East, with two regional officials saying the U.S. has moved many of its assets out of the Persian Gulf. That includes aircraft, air defense systems, communications systems and other equipment crucial to base operations, one of those officials said.

The impact of the damage raises questions about American defenses in the region as President Donald Trump considers new strikes after Tuesday's midterm elections and Tehran has vowed major retaliation. A return to hostilities threatens additional costly damage to bases, which would heighten uncertainty about whether the United States will choose to rebuild its bases and equipment in the region when the war ends.

The AP's analysis offers new insight into Iran's strategy for its retaliation and what precisely has been damaged on U.S. bases during the eight-month war, going beyond the details that have been released in independent reviews, including from the Pentagon's inspector general . It found that from April 1 to June 30, Iranian strikes had damaged and destroyed hundreds of buildings and other structures on U.S. bases.

Such assessments provide the only overall snapshot because the Trump administration and the U.S. military have provided few details about the toll of the conflict on people and equipment, even putting measures in place to impede outside review, such as delays in the release of satellite images.

U.S. Central Command, which oversees operations in the Middle East, has refused to comment on or specify damage to bases or equipment, usually citing the need for operational security. The command did not comment for this story.

Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell asserted that U.S. "forces and bases are well protected and America's military is stronger than ever."

"Our service members in CENTCOM have everything they need to continue their historic success ensuring Iran never obtains a nuclear weapon," Parnell said in a statement to the AP.

Here's what Iran targeted at US bases in the Middle East

Most of the Iranian attacks have been in Kuwait, while U.S. sites in Bahrain, Iraq, Jordan, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates also have been targeted, the analysis of satellite imagery shows. The deadliest known strike on U.S. troops in the Iran war was in Kuwait, where six soldiers were killed in a drone attack at Port Shuaiba on March 1.

Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait was struck at least 30 times, damaging or destroying at least 15 aircraft hangars, numerous warehouses and 10 buildings near a residential area.

Camp Buehring, also in Kuwait, faced even heavier losses. While Iranian attacks made most of its hangars inoperable, gathering places for troops sustained much more damage because the base had limited aircraft. Its gym was destroyed in March and a store for troops to buy products on the base was hit in late July.

A strike also has severely damaged the garage and dining room there, according to the two regional officials. They and two others, who are regional military officials, spoke to the AP on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive details about the damage to bases.

While strikes were much heavier against Iran, American matériel losses were inevitable, said Raphael Cohen, director of the National Security Program at the RAND School of Public Policy. The way wars are fought today makes all militaries "susceptible to large-scale, cheap drone attacks," he said.

"This should be a wake-up call for the United States," Cohen said.

Iran focused on targeting US systems meant to detect incoming strikes

Iran launched its response to the war with accurate attacks on systems meant to detect and thwart incoming strikes, then broadened its targets to buildings and equipment that made U.S. bases useful and habitable.

Iran destroyed enclosures protecting U.S. radar systems at Camp Arifjan in Kuwait and Naval Support Activity Bahrain within the first two days of the war's start in late February. Additionally, Iran hit portable radars at Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia and Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan.

Iran prioritized striking at the backbone of the U.S. air defense system, targeting key early-warning radars that are difficult and expensive to repair or replace, said N.R. Jenzen-Jones, director of the technical intelligence consulting firm Armament Research Services.

A radar was hit in Jordan and said to be destroyed. It was one of only 13 possessed by the Army globally, manufacturer Raytheon said. Budget documents show each costs about half a billion dollars.

Another radar in Qatar was damaged significantly, but it is unclear if it was destroyed. Purchased by the Gulf country in a 2013 deal valued at $1.1 billion, it appears to have been the only one in the region.

Hitting such sites was likely "intended to disrupt and degrade the U.S. and allies' ability to respond to further strikes," Jenzen-Jones said.

After hitting the radars, Iran launched more than 50 successful strikes on 18 locations with U.S. military equipment in the first month of the war, prioritizing areas with aircraft.

Iran damaged refueling aircraft, communication systems, fuel bunkers and troop accommodations at various bases, the two regional officials said. An Iranian strike on Prince Sultan Air Base in March damaged the back half of a Boeing E-3 Sentry surveillance aircraft and another hit a CIA unit at the U.S. Embassy in Riyadh.

A separate regional military official, who recently visited the Saudi air base, described a severely damaged facility with scattered debris and broken construction materials. He said he saw damaged equipment, including bombed-out barracks and mess halls.

The official said the attack that hit the surveillance plane also damaged several other aircraft, including two aerial refueling tankers. A Congressional Research Service report updated in October said 15 U.S. aircraft had been damaged on regional bases.

Al Dhafra Air Base, about 20 miles (32 kilometers) south of Abu Dhabi in the UAE, was hit frequently early in the war, according to a second regional military official with direct knowledge of the damage. The official noted damage to infrastructure like aircraft hangars and other installations as well as to equipment such as an early-warning radar system and surveillance drones.

Major providers with U.S. contracts have blocked or delayed public release of satellite imagery at the request of American officials, who sometimes cited it being a national security risk. That has left limited options to visually confirm strike damage until imagery could be obtained from OneAtlas, a satellite provider owned by Airbus.

In the example of Camp Buehring in Kuwait, one of the hardest-hit bases, high-quality imagery from reliable providers was not available until late August. From the halt of imagery in early March to its reemergence in August, more than 30 structures on the base were damaged or destroyed. The AP confirmed that Iran struck Camp Buehring numerous times in March, April, May and July.

Months later, no endgame for the war has been articulated, and more damage could be ahead if hostilities resume, which the U.S. and Iran both say is possible.

The conflict could foreshadow a new reality for U.S. forces.

"This is the operating environment that we're going to face in the future," said Cohen, the RAND analyst. "The idea that we can rely on fixed infrastructure in the way that we have during the global war on terrorism is over."

articles.title: From asses to masses, Republicans wonder if Trump can still deliver wins
articles.summary: TOI Correspondent from Washington: US President Donald Trump has spent an extraordinary amount of campaign time discussing the physique of other public
articles.body: TOI Correspondent from Washington: US President Donald Trump has spent an extraordinary amount of campaign time discussing the physique of other public figures, including their butts, legs, and other physical attributes. While the Republican Party supremo may be preoccupied with posteriors and treating his MAGA masses to jokes about asses, GOP candidates have a rather more pressing anatomical question: does Trump still have legs to carry them over the line in the midterms elections?Indeed, the MAGA boss is getting huffy about the physical toll and relentless schedule of the campaign trail and is now approaching it with the enthusiasm of a man who has just been informed that his prison sentence has been extended. "I thought this was going to be my last one. I thought I could relax. Twenty-eight days in a row of this crap is a lot. My voice is operating at about 49.2%," he grumbled at a rally in Florida on Friday, complaining, "So on Sunday, while you're all watching football, I'll be traveling in a very beautiful airplane to Iowa, to Kansas."It takes a peculiar sense of self-deprecation to describe one’s own rallies as “crap,” but this is Trump. At another rally last month, he offered an astonishingly candid description of his relationship with his followers, saying, "I could say the stupidest thing, and y'all would just laugh and clap." The question political pundits are trying to figure out is at what point does his MAGA faithful wake up to being told the rallies they flock to are “crap,” and they are possibly stupid. Right now, there is little evidence they have abandoned their leader in large numbers, although there are signs the sheen is wearing off.At a Trump rally in South Carolina last week, a man approached by Fox News was asked the perfectly innocuous question: Why are you here? "Well, in the late 70s, I was a little too young to go to South America for the Jonestown Massacre. But this is as close as I'll ever get…There's nothing like seeing a cult right up front," he said. The reference was to the 1978 incident in Guyana, when more than 900 followers of cult leader Jim Jones died in a mass murder-suicide episode unparalleled in modern history. The reporter, who had assumed the man, a former Republican, was a Trump supporter, bolted in embarrassment to find someone else to interview.Invoking the Jim Jones cult was an unusually savage description of MAGA faithful, but it also captured a question increasingly confronting Republicans as America heads to polling stations on Tuesday: Is Trump's political movement still an electoral coalition, or has it become a congregation whose members would applaud even if the pastor preaches violence?Yet this is the peculiar political chemistry of MAGA; Trump knows his audience, and his audience knows him. Their relationship is not necessarily built on policy consistency, intellectual coherence or even conventional political expectations; It is built on identity, grievance, resentment and an enduring conviction that Trump, however outrageous, is fighting their battles despite stories of grift and corruption Washington is now awash with.There is also a generational divide that is becoming increasingly visible. At rallies and in interviews, parents and children sometimes find themselves on opposite sides of the Trump phenomenon. Younger family members challenge the president's rhetoric and politics, while their parents remain devoted supporters. Trump has repeatedly turned this domestic disagreement into a campaign punchline, telling younger people, in effect, that their parents vote for him. It is a useful reminder that MAGA is not simply a political preference; For many, it has become an identity, strong enough to survive Thanksgiving dinner, family arguments, and interventions by offsprings armed with a smartphone and fact-check.The generational friction has also become lucrative entertainment for many liberal podcasters and social-media influencers who have discovered that interviewing committed Trump supporters, asking seemingly straightforward questions, and allowing the answers to speak for themselves can generate enormous online engagement. The format is simple: find a MAGA dope, ask about a policy, a political contradiction or an extraordinary presidential statement, and let the conversation unfold. The audience is invited to laugh, cringe or marvel because interviewee often appears oblivious to the fact that the exchange is being consumed as comedy rather than political persuasion.Vivek Ramaswamy, the Indian-American Republican gubernatorial hopeful in Ohio, recently discovered how easily these encounters can be weaponised. During an interaction, a man confronted him with a question about why a pedophile appeared in one of his campaign advertisements. Ramaswamy initially looked bewildered, attempted to respond and eventually walked away as the exchange circulated online. Whether it is a carefully staged prank or an opportunistic ambush, the point is that Republican politicians are increasingly encountering an opposition that understands the economics of viral embarrassment.And Trump himself continues to supply the material. The president's own rallies have become an increasingly unpredictable mixture of political campaigning, stand-up comedy, grievance therapy -- and occasionally, an anatomy lecture even as his party’s ass is on line come November 3.You use AI every day. articles.body: NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Saturday staunchly criticised the opposition for "choosing to be an obstructionists" after a decade of despair and frustration emanating from the intermittent electoral routs.PM Modi said the opposition has made obstruction "a core" of its politics, while taking a veiled swipe at Congress leader Rahul Gandhi over abroad trips."These forces are continuously engaged in conspiracies to divide the country. Vicious plots are being hatched to divide and instigate conflict among the children of Mother India. Driven by more than a decade of frustration and disappointment, these people have now come out into the open. Who is secretly meeting whom abroad? Which anti-India forces are supporting them? Who is speaking the language of India's enemies? We must recognise all these patterns. We must confront them unitedly," PM Modi was quoted as saying by news agency ANI.PM Modi said anti-India forces had become active amid a global energy crisis and slammed the Opposition, saying it had turned into “Avrodh Paksh” (obstructive force) rather than “Virodh Paksh” (opposing group).Accusing opposition of ripping apart the dignity and boundaries of the Constitution, PM Modi said: "Social media is being weaponised to spread rumours and to malign India's image. The citizens of the country must handle this together. We have eliminated Naxalism in far-flung areas, but the threat of 'Dimagi Naxalism' has not yet been averted from the nation. The country must always remain alert to these 'Dimagi Naxals'..."PM Modi also alleged that "certain forces inside the country were busy trying to create instability by spreading lies and rumours"."However, the citizens stood shoulder to shoulder with the nation. This is the greatest strength of this country, and it serves as the ultimate foundation for our courage," he said in Gujarat.PM Modi said hailed nation's resilience amidst global headwinds, and said that despite widespread disruptions and an escalating international fuel crunch, it is a "testament to India's capability" that the country ensured its citizens remained protected from the brunt of the global energy crisis.Addressing the gathering on Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel’s 151st birth anniversary, the Prime Minister also pointed out how several nations struggled with fuel supplies while dire predictions were made regarding India.Earlier, PM Modi paid floral tributes at the Statue of Unity in Ekta Nagar, accompanied by an aerial flower petal shower by Indian Air Force helicopters.Later, he participated at the Rashtriya Ekta Diwas celebrations at the Parade Ground, administered the unity pledge, and reviewed the Ekta Parade comprising multiple marching contingents.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: More than 5,000 die from Ebola in DR Congo's deadliest outbreak
articles.summary: Government data shows that more than 10,000 people have contracted the rare virus.
articles.body:
More than 5,000 people have died from an ongoing Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo, government data shows.

Eight of 26 provinces are now affected, with more than 10,300 confirmed cases.

The outbreak, which started in May, became the country's deadliest in its history in August, public health officials said. The current case fatality rate is 48.6%.

In its latest update, the health ministry said the epicentre of the epidemic remains in the Ituri province, in the north-east of the country, which is a conflict zone, making it harder to contain the virus.

Cases have also been confirmed in Kenya, Nigeria and Uganda.

This marks the 17th outbreak in DR Congo's history, according to the United Nations (UN), and the second largest in history.

The World Health Organization (WHO) office in Africa said a "continued scale-up of key control measures, greater access to affected areas, and community outreach" is needed to end the outbreak.

Testing and treatment are under way, along with clinical trials of vaccines, it added.

The Bundibugyo species is behind the current outbreak, but there is not yet any treatment or vaccine for this strain.

DR Congo's previous deadliest outbreak saw 2,299 deaths recorded between 2018-2020, the UN said.

The deadliest in history occurred in West Africa between 2014 and 2016, killing more than 11,325 people and spread across several countries, including Italy, the UK and United States, according to the WHO.

The UN warns that the current outbreak is "taking lives at a much faster rate".

Ebola is a rare, deadly disease caused by a virus, and symptoms come on suddenly.

As the disease progresses, vomiting and diarrhoea develop and it can lead to organ failure. Some, but not all, patients develop internal and external bleeding.

The virus spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.

Adding to the challenge of treating the disease, some health workers and a politician have been attacked while responding to the outbreak.

Earlier this week, a nurse was killed and another health worker seriously injured in an attack when responding to an Ebola alert. Local youths had accused them of contaminating water sources and spreading the virus, according to the UN-backed Radio Okapi.

Last month, a politician was beaten to death after promoting measures to stop the spread of Ebola, while in August, the Red Cross said its volunteers had been injured and an ambulance set on fire in 11 violent incidents in the outbreak's first 100 days.

In Uganda, two people died and 20 cases were recorded shortly after the outbreak started, but no cases have been reported since August. Travel restrictions remain in place for those crossing into the country from neighbouring DR Congo.

In Kenya, there have been nine confirmed cases and two recorded deaths.

Two suspected cases were identified in Nigeria on Saturday, its disease control centre said, adding that the individuals have been isolated and they are undergoing testing.

Earlier in October, one woman was confirmed to have the disease in the country but was flown to Switzerland for further treatment.

The likelihood of infection for people in the Europe area is "very low," the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control said.

articles.title: Daylight Saving Time ends tonight: When to change your clocks? When do we spring forward in 2027?
articles.summary: Millions of Americans will gain an extra hour of sleep this weekend as Daylight Saving Time comes to an end for 2026.
articles.body: Millions of Americans will gain an extra hour of sleep this weekend as Daylight Saving Time comes to an end for 2026. Clocks across most of the United States will move back by one hour overnight, marking the return to standard time. The annual change will take place on Sunday, November 1, at 2 am local time, when clocks will roll back to 1 am.The change means Americans will get an additional hour in their day, with sunrise and sunset occurring earlier according to the clock. While smartphones, computers and other internet-connected devices generally adjust automatically, people using traditional clocks and watches will need to change them manually.The transition will also affect the time difference between the US and other countries, including India, as American cities move back one hour. New York will move from 9 hours 30 minutes behind India to 10 hours 30 minutes behind India.When does Daylight Saving Time end in 2026?Daylight Saving Time officially ends at 2 am on Sunday, November 1, 2026, across most of the US.Under the current federal schedule, clocks are moved back one hour at 2 am local time, meaning the time becomes 1 am again. The hour between 1 am and 2 am will therefore occur twice.People who want to adjust their clocks manually can do so before going to bed on Saturday night. Most smartphones, computers and other digital devices connected to automatic time settings will make the adjustment without requiring any action from users.The US follows the practice of moving clocks forward in March and backward in November. The system is commonly remembered through the phrase "spring forward, fall back".Which states do not observe Daylight Saving Time?Although most of the country follows Daylight Saving Time, there are exceptions.Hawaii and most of Arizona do not observe the seasonal clock change and remain on standard time throughout the year. However, the Navajo Nation, which extends into parts of Arizona, observes Daylight Saving Time.Several US territories also do not follow the practice. These include American Samoa, Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands, Puerto Rico and the US Virgin Islands.For residents in areas that observe DST, the November 1 change means clocks will move back one hour. Those living in locations that do not observe it will continue following their existing time.When does Daylight Saving Time start again in 2027?Daylight Saving Time will return on Sunday, March 14, 2027, in areas that observe the seasonal clock change.The transition will happen at 2 am local time, when clocks will jump forward to 3 am. Unlike the November adjustment, Americans will lose an hour of sleep during the spring transition.The change will bring longer daylight hours in the evening, with sunsets occurring an hour later according to the clock.The US follows a federal schedule under which Daylight Saving Time begins on the second Sunday of March and ends on the first Sunday of November. The current dates were established through the Energy Policy Act of 2005 and came into effect in 2007.Why does the US change its clocks twice a year?Daylight Saving Time is a practice of moving clocks forward by one hour during part of the year to extend daylight into the evening.The idea is to make better use of daylight during the warmer months, when the sun rises earlier. By moving clocks forward in spring, people get more daylight after typical working hours, although mornings become darker.When clocks move back in November, daylight shifts back towards the morning hours. This means people generally experience earlier sunrises and sunsets according to the clock.The US first introduced Daylight Saving Time nationally in 1918 during World War I, partly as an effort to conserve fuel. The practice was later repealed and reintroduced, with Congress eventually establishing uniform rules through the Uniform Time Act of 1966.The current schedule was expanded in 2007, extending the period of Daylight Saving Time by several weeks.Will the US stop changing clocks permanently?The twice-yearly clock change has remained a subject of political debate in the US, with supporters arguing that permanent Daylight Saving Time would eliminate disruptions caused by changing clocks.President Donald Trump has supported making Daylight Saving Time permanent. The Sunshine Protection Act, which seeks to make the change permanent, passed the House of Representatives in July 2026 by a 308-117 vote. However, it has not secured Senate approval.Senate Majority Leader John Thune has indicated that there is no consensus or clear path forward for the legislation. As a result, the existing clock-changing schedule remains in place for now.Critics of permanent Daylight Saving Time argue that winter mornings would become darker, potentially affecting schoolchildren, commuters and workers. Supporters say longer evening daylight would benefit businesses, recreation and everyday activities.Unless Congress changes the law, Americans in areas that observe Daylight Saving Time will continue to move their clocks forward in March and back in November. For now, the next change is scheduled for March 14, 2027.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: In 1924, a donated New York gorge became Buttermilk Falls State Park; 102 years later, a land trust paid $1.3 million for a nearby four-acre family homestead to pave the way for better park access and trails
articles.summary: More than a century after a generous land donation helped create Buttermilk Falls State Park, a small but important piece of its neighboring landscape is
articles.body: More than a century after a generous land donation helped create Buttermilk Falls State Park, a small but important piece of its neighboring landscape is being returned to public use. The Open Space Institute has acquired a four-acre property between the park’s existing entrance and Route 13 in Tompkins County for $1.3 million, purchasing it from the Margaret M. Rumsey Trust, as per their website. The organisation plans to transfer the land to the New York State Office of Parks, Recreation and Historic Preservation as an addition to Buttermilk Falls State Park. The property includes a former bed-and-breakfast and sits at the foot of the gorge that gave the park its name. Once transferred, it could support a redesigned park gateway with reconfigured parking, improved traffic circulation, better wayfinding, housing for staff, and a new trailhead. For a park that welcomes nearly 400,000 visitors each year, the acquisition represents an opportunity to make access safer, smoother, and more welcoming. Read more about it here, as per Open Space Institute:A park born from a family giftButtermilk Falls State Park traces its origins to 1924, when Hugh E. Rumsey and his partner, Robert H. Treman, divided a larger family property. Mr. and Mrs. Treman then donated the gorge and surrounding hillside to New York State, creating Buttermilk Falls State Park. The park now covers more than 800 acres and includes waterfalls, gorge trails, a swimming area, picnic grounds, woodlands, and open spaces.The newly acquired homestead has a direct connection to that history. Dave Rumsey, speaking for the Margaret M. Rumsey Trust, said the Federal-style brick house was built around 1825 at the foot of Buttermilk Falls. It was originally part of a larger farm that included Buttermilk Creek and its gorge, where cows watered long before Margaret Rumsey worked as a lifeguard.Margaret Rumsey later converted the brick house into the Buttermilk Falls Bed and Breakfast in 1983. She operated it until a few years before her death in 2021. The Rumsey family said they believe Margaret would be pleased to see the homestead, where she raised her sons and welcomed guests, transitioned for use alongside the park she loved.Why the four acres matterThe property may be small, but its location makes it valuable. It lies between the park’s current entrance and Route 13, a busy corridor that can create congestion and access challenges during busy periods. The Open Space Institute says the site is expected to become a future trailhead and parking area, expanding existing park improvements and easing pressure during peak visitation times.The acquisition also creates room for better traffic flow and clearer visitor navigation. With more people visiting New York’s state parks each year, the organization says thoughtful improvements are needed to help people connect with nature without overwhelming the places they come to enjoy. The four acres preserve an opportunity to expand parking capacity while improving the overall visitor experience.The former bed-and-breakfast could eventually serve another practical purpose. OSI says the structure may house AmeriCorps service members who support Buttermilk Falls State Park and other parks across the Finger Lakes region. During OSI’s ownership, the organization will maintain all structures on the property and work with state parks officials to assess future needs.Connecting a growing trail networkThe land acquisition is also part of a larger effort to connect parks and trails across the Finger Lakes. Buttermilk Falls State Park is a key anchor in long-term plans for multi-use trails and public transportation, including the in-development Black Diamond Trail expansion. That project is intended to ultimately connect Taughannock Falls State Park, Allan H. Treman State Marine Park, Buttermilk Falls State Park, and Robert H. Treman State Park.More than eight miles of rail trail have already been built by state and local partners, with additional connections underway. OSI says the new property preserves an important opportunity to expand access to that broader recreational network. A new trailhead could make it easier for visitors to move between parks, explore longer routes, and reach the region’s natural attractions without relying solely on cars.The New York State Office of Parks, Recreation and Historic Preservation has identified conservation of the property as a high priority for the Finger Lakes region. Executive Deputy Commissioner Tom Alworth said the future addition of the parcel is an example of how New York is expanding outdoor recreation, improving visitor access, and protecting the environment for both visitors and neighbors.Protecting land and expanding accessThe Open Space Institute has been working on land conservation since 1974 and says it has helped protect more than 2.5 million acres of at-risk and environmentally sensitive land across the eastern United States. Its work supports clean air and water, wildlife habitat, recreation, and community resilience against extreme weather. The Buttermilk Falls acquisition fits that broader mission by protecting land while also improving public access.OSI President and CEO Erik Kulleseid said the organisation is helping ensure that New York’s state parks can meet the changing needs of the people who use them. He described the acquisition as creating new possibilities for thoughtful improvements that will help visitors better connect with nature.The site will remain closed to the public while OSI owns it, but its future role could be significant. A place that once welcomed overnight guests as a family-run bed-and-breakfast may soon help welcome hundreds of thousands of annual visitors to one of New York’s most beloved state parks. articles.title: Skipper who champions Cornish sardines gets national award
articles.summary: Tom Lambourn is praised by judges for his efforts to ensure stocks remain healthy.
articles.body:
A skipper who champions sustainable Cornish sardines has been named Fishing Hero of the Year at a national awards ceremony.

Tom Lambourn, from Newlyn, Cornwall, received the Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) UK award at a gala dinner at London's Fishmongers' Hall earlier this week.

He was recognised by the judges for his dedication to promoting the small scale Cornish sardine fishery.

In his acceptance speech, Lambourn said it was "brilliant to be part of a sustainable fishery".

The 30-year-old skipper, who left the coastal town to study for a chemistry degree, said he was drawn back by the pull of the ocean and now captains his own sardine boat, the Lyonesse, throughout the sardine season from July to April.

Lambourn was also credited for a decision taken by Paradise Park to feed their penguins Cornish sardines rather than sprats.

He said: "I'm really proud to accept this award and represent the fantastic Cornish sardine fishery.

"Sustainable fishing means that the future generations of my family will also be able to fish.

"It's so important to educate young people about the importance of the MSC and being certified."

Lewis Tattersall, MSC UK and Ireland senior fisheries outreach manager, said: "The judges could not help but be impressed by Tom's enthusiasm and effectiveness in championing the product he and his crew land but also the lengths to which they go to ensure stocks remain healthy and the Cornish coastline and its abundant sea life remains pristine.

"Tom is a very worthy Fishing Hero of the Year."

articles.title: INDIA bloc 'impeaches' CEC in mock Parliament, but what will it take to remove him for real
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The opposition on Saturday unanimously passed a \"resolution\" to remove Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over allegations of
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The opposition on Saturday unanimously passed a "resolution" to remove Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over allegations of irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls during a "mock Parliament" organised at Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge's residence.Former Lok Sabha Speaker Meira Kumar presided over the proceedings, with several MPs and activists supporting the demand for the CEC's removal.Kharge moved the resolution seeking Kumar's removal, accusing him of centralising control over electoral rolls and acting at the behest of Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Union home minister Amit Shah. Kharge also said that SIR was initiated to remove voters opposed to Bharatiya Janata Party."The proposal we are bringing today is to safeguard the dignity of a constitutional institution. We have no personal enmity with the CEC. Our intention is that the Election Commission should function impartially in keeping with the spirit of the Constitution," Kharge said."The trust of the common man in it should remain intact. No one sitting in Delhi should be able to wrongly delete the voting rights of weaker sections, women, and youth using a computer," he added.Meanwhile, leader of opposition in Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi delivered the closing remarks of the proceedings, describing the event as the opposition's political weapon targeting CEC Gyanesh Kumar, PM Modi and Amit Shah."This looks like a meeting of Lok Sabha MPs, Rajya Sabha MPs, and common citizens. But actually, this is a political weapon," Rahul said.In the "mock Parliament" at Kharge's residence, the opposition sailed through the resolution with a voice vote. But while the numbers may have been on its side there, would the same motion stand a chance in the real Parliament?What will it take to remove CEC Gyanesh Kumar for realThe removal of a CEC is deliberately difficult.Article 324(5) of the Constitution states that the Chief Election Commissioner can be removed from office only "in like manner and on the like grounds as a judge of the Supreme Court.""The other Election Commissioners shall not be removed from office except on the recommendation of the Chief Election Commissioner," it further says.Article 124(4) of the Constitution, which lays down the procedure for removing a Supreme Court judge, states that a judge can be removed only by an order of the President following an address by each House of Parliament.Such an address must be supported by a majority of the total membership of that House and by a majority of at least two-thirds of members present and voting, in the same session, on the ground of proved misbehaviour or incapacity.The process begins with a notice of motion in either House of Parliament alleging misbehaviour or incapacity. The notice must be signed by at least 100 MPs in the Lok Sabha or 50 MPs in the Rajya Sabha.The presiding officer of the concerned House can admit or refuse the motion after considering the material and information available. If the motion is admitted, an inquiry is conducted into the charges by a committee constituted for the purpose.If the charges are established, the motion must be passed by a majority of the total membership of each House and by a two-thirds majority of members present and voting in both Houses.Once both Houses pass the motion in accordance with these requirements, an address is made to the President, who then issues the order removing the CEC.The President's role at this stage is constitutional and formal once Parliament has passed the required address.Interestingly, this is not the first time when the opposition is gearing up for introducing a resolution seeking CEC's removal.On April 7, Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla and Rajya Sabha Chairperson CP Radhakrishnan had rejected opposition notice, which was signed by 130 Lok Sabha members, 63 Rajya Sabha members, seeking the CEC's removal over alleged partisanship and arbitrariness in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: 'Will deal with Modi, Shah': Rahul Gandhi explains why CEC Gyanesh Kumar his first target
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Union home minister Amit Shah may be at the top of the political chain of command, but Rahul Gandhi has made
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Union home minister Amit Shah may be at the top of the political chain of command, but Rahul Gandhi has made it clear that the opposition's first target is Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar.Explaining why the INDIA bloc has upped its attack on the election chief, the Congress leader accused him of acting as an instrument of the ruling establishment and warned that those allegedly involved in undermining democratic institutions would be held accountable."Mr Modi and Mr Shah might be on top. We will deal with them, but you are their instruments, and so you are our first target," Rahul Gandhi said on Saturday at the INDIA bloc event in Delhi, where opposition leaders held a symbolic public impeachment of Gyanesh Kumar.The leader of opposition in the Lok Sabha warned the CEC and other officials against assuming that constitutional immunity would shield them from accountability."So if Mr Gyanesh Kumar thinks, or the five or seven people below him think, that immunity will save them, I would kindly suggest to them, with love and affection, to take a look at what is going on in the country. Please understand the mood of the people outside. You will see tomorrow itself," he said.Rahul Gandhi was referring to the opposition's planned march and public rally in Delhi on Sunday, which he described as an opportunity for a united opposition to demonstrate public anger over alleged electoral irregularities."A united opposition is going to show you exactly what the mood of the people of this country is," he said.'We are not going to let you escape'Rahul Gandhi said the opposition's action against CEC was not an isolated protest against one constitutional functionary but part of a larger fight over what he alleged was the misuse of democratic institutions."You can continue to rig the elections. You can continue to control and allow the misuse of the CBI, the ED, and every single institution of this country. But we guarantee you that this is a temporary phenomenon," he said.The Congress leader insisted that Gyanesh Kumar was only one among several people the opposition held responsible for what it described as an assault on the country's democratic institutions."We are not going to let you escape. I also want to address the people who have carried out this assault on the Union of India. Gyanesh Kumar is just one element; there are many others. We know who they are, and we understand deeply who they are," Rahul Gandhi said."This is a warning to you: things are shifting. Please hear this warning and realise that this is a new political weapon sitting in the garden, and this weapon is going to hurt you very badly if you continue down your path," he said."I am saying this with love and affection; we are not nasty or evil people, but we will protect the Constitution and the voice of our people."Rahul Gandhi also backed the demand for legal action against the CEC, saying Gyanesh Kumar should not only face impeachment but also be tried in court for treason."I fully support the motion that Mr Gyanesh Kumar should not only be impeached but should also be tried in a court of law for treason so that justice can be served," he said.INDIA bloc holds 'public impeachment' of CECRahul Gandhi's remarks came at an unprecedented INDIA bloc event in which opposition MPs and leaders, along with civil society representatives, passed a resolution seeking Gyanesh Kumar's impeachment and accusing him of facilitating the deletion of voters' names to influence election outcomes.The symbolic proceedings were held at the lawns of Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge's residence at 10, Rajaji Marg in New Delhi. Former Lok Sabha Speaker Meira Kumar presided over the meeting, which was organised in a setting resembling parliamentary proceedings.The resolution was moved by Kharge, seconded by Samajwadi Party leader Harendra Malik and supported by Rahul Gandhi and several other opposition MPs and civil society members. It was adopted unanimously by a show of hands.Around 250 opposition MPs, civil society representatives and mediapersons attended the event. Some people who alleged that their names had been wrongly deleted from electoral rolls were also present.Rahul Gandhi acknowledged that holding what resembled parliamentary proceedings outside Parliament might appear unusual, but said the opposition had been left with little choice."I don't think anything like this has ever happened in history," he said, adding that the gathering of opposition leaders and civil society members in a garden might appear absurd."But we had no other option, as every single institution is closed to us," he said.The stage was designed to resemble the old Lok Sabha chamber, with a wooden-panelled backdrop and seats arranged in a semi-circular formation.Kharge, who moved the motion, alleged that the right to vote was under threat because the Election Commission was functioning at the behest of PM Modi and Shah. He accused the poll panel of failing to act independently and raised concerns over alleged electoral manipulation.BJP calls it 'mockery' of democracyThe BJP hit back at the opposition's symbolic proceedings, accusing the INDIA bloc of making a mockery of Parliament and democratic institutions.BJP spokesperson Sambit Patra took a swipe at Rahul Gandhi, alleging that the Congress was repeatedly attempting to launch its leader politically without success."Go ahead and hold your mock Parliament or take out your marches; the world has already understood that Rahul Gandhi simply lacks the fuel. This 'satellite' is never going to launch," Patra said.He added that the opposition could have Gandhi as a "mock Prime Minister for life".Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: John Healey risks breaking minimum wage promise for younger workers
articles.summary: The Chancellor has suggested that younger workers might not receive the same minimum wage as others before the next election.
articles.body:
The Chancellor, John Healey, has suggested that younger workers might not receive the same minimum wage as others before the next election, potentially breaking a Labour manifesto promise.

In 2024, Labour said it would remove "discriminatory age bands", vowing to end the gap between the adult minimum wage and pay for 18 to 20-year-olds.

But in last week's Budget, Healey said that younger workers would see the same increase as older workers, leaving a gap between the two rates this year.

Pay for 18 to 20-year-olds in 2026 will rise to £11.27, while over-20s will be paid a minimum of £13.21 an hour.

In a BBC interview to be broadcast on Sunday , Healey was asked if younger workers would be paid the same as older workers, when it comes to the minimum wage, by the time of the next election?

"We'll take one step at a time," he said, suggesting that Labour might abandon its plan to close the gap before the next election.

It is a change that is likely to anger the unions and some on the left of the party.

Healey added that Labour was still committed to the ambition, but hinted the plan to equalise wages might be delayed, partly to encourage businesses to employ younger workers.

"There is no question about whether or if, it's a question of when - it's a question of how fast," he said.

"I want to make sure we can look hard at those trade-offs that are there between jobs and wages."

"I want to take business, I want to take trade unions with me, and with the government, because together we have to get into what at the moment is a moral shame on this nation. A million youngsters - written off without any prospect of being helped into work and making contributions to this country for the future."

The chancellor also suggested that he is willing to make potentially big cuts to some areas of public spending, to get the country's debt falling.

The budget documents spell out real-terms reductions to some government departments in the years to come.

The likelihood of the government following through was questioned by the respected independent number cruncher, the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) this week.

But asked if he would make big cuts, Healey said: "We've already demonstrated we are prepared to take hard decisions about the priorities in government."

Pressed on whether he would make cuts of more than 2% a year to some government departments, he added: "We will carry that through to the 10-year plan and the spending review next year."

"But in the budget I also set out the ways that we're preparing and the work we've got under way to prepare for those spending review decisions."

articles.title: Ramkund finds its rhythm again as Simhastha Kumbh begins
articles.summary: Ramkund in Nashik revives as Simhastha Kumbh begins, with Godavari water restored and President Droupadi Murmu hoisting the Dharma Dhwaja.
articles.body: Nashik: Hours before President Droupadi Murmu hoisted the Dharma Dhwaja at Ramkund on Saturday, the Simhastha Kumbh Mela had already arrived in spirit.From early morning, devotees streamed towards Godavari ghats. By the time President reached Ramkund shortly after 11 am, the riverfront had turned into a sea of devotees, flowers and anticipation. Conch shells echoed across the ghats. Vedic chants mingled with cries of “Jai Shri Ram” and “Shivaji Maharaj Ki Jai”. Every available vantage point was occupied.The transformation was striking.For nearly three months, Ramkund, Laxman Kund and Sita Kund had remained largely dry as infrastructure works progressed along the riverfront. On Saturday, however, water once again flowed through the historic stretch after a release from Gangapur dam, restoring the familiar sight of Godavari winding past flower-decked ghats and ancient temples.The preparations had begun the previous night. Temples and ghats glowed under decorative lighting. Floral arrangements adorned the ceremonial area, while tableaux depicting Samudra Manthan drew visitors. Security barricades and checkpoints lined approach roads, but beyond them, the atmosphere was that of a festival long awaited.Among those drawing attention were 24-year-olds Gaurav Pandey and Vaishnavi Atram, dressed as Lord Ram and Sita. As they moved through the crowd, devotees stopped them for photographs, touched their feet and sought blessings.“We are associated with Shri Ram Seva Samiti and dress as Lord Ram and Sita during major religious events,” Pandey said. “People’s devotion and affection make the effort worthwhile,” he added.The ceremony also attracted visitors from outside India. James Harper, a tourist from England, travelled to Nashik after learning about Dhwajarohan.“I was in Mumbai when I heard about the ceremony and decided to come here,” he said. “Everything is beautifully organised. Despite the huge crowd, movement has been remarkably smooth,” he said.As noon approached, the anticipation deepened. Eyes turned towards the 51-foot Dhwajstambh while priests conducted rituals at the yagya kund and performed worship of Godavari and the ceremonial flag.Then came the moment thousands had gathered to witness.At exactly 12.02 pm, President Murmu hoisted the Dharma Dhwaja. As the flag unfurled above Godavari, conches sounded, bells rang and chants rose from the crowd. Sadhus, mahants, devotees and dignitaries looked on as the fluttering flag formally announced the beginning of the once-in-12-years pilgrimage.For Ramkund, the day was about more than a ceremony. articles.title: Rising road levels worsen monsoon woes in city’s western suburbs
articles.summary: Chennai western suburbs face monsoon flooding as roads rise from repeated relaying without milling, leaving homes below road level and lacking stormwater drains.
articles.body: Chennai: For residents of Iyyappanthangal, Kattupakkam, Thelliyar Agaram and Karayanchavadi, every monsoon brings the fear of rainwater entering their homes, as roads outside their houses continue to rise with repeated relaying without milling.In several stretches, road levels are now at least 2 ft higher than floor level of buildings, leaving homes and parking spaces vulnerable to flooding. With many neighbourhoods also lacking stormwater drains, residents say even moderate rainfall can leave roads and houses inundated.At least 80 interior roads, including Parani Puthur Main Road, Kundrathur High Road, Old Porur Road and Kummananchavadi High Road, are higher than the floor levels of adjoining buildings. Residents say several stretches were re-laid about six months ago, with fresh wet-mix laid over existing surfaces without milling the old road.According to the official data, at least 36 low-lying locations are identified as hotspots and are prone to inundation during monsoon. The areas, with an estimated combined population of two lakh, also fall within a wider canal network that carries water from Kosasthalaiyar basin towards Porur lake and eventually Adyar river.According to the Tamil Nadu Panchayats Act, 1994, for village panchayats to maintain local roads and public infrastructure, the roads should not be re-laid without being milled.“In the last three years, 200 interior roads have been relaid without milling. In many areas, residents had to spend at least Rs 1.5 lakh to raise their car parking levels. Whenever complaints are raised about water stagnation, officials simply raise the road level instead of constructing stormwater drains. This issue needs to be addressed at the earliest,” said P Senthil Kumar, a social activist and resident of Iyyappanthangal.“For years, we have been asking panchayat officials to construct stormwater drains, but our concerns have been ignored. articles.summary: Southern Naval Command announces Navy Day 2024 events in Kochi: base visits, photo exhibition, Dec 3 naval ops demo, and Dec 4 concert.
articles.body: Kochi: Southern Naval Command (SNC) on Thursday announced details of Navy Day-related activities for the year.These activities will commence in Nov and culminate with the Naval Operations Demonstration at Kochi on Dec 3, followed by Navy Day on Dec 4.On Nov 16, Naval Base will welcome special children and senior citizens followed by invited school students on Nov 23. The visits will offer participants an opportunity to experience naval life at close quarters through visits to naval ships and INS Garuda, as well as a display of weapons, equipment and models of ships and aircraft. These initiatives are intended to familiarise visitors with Navy’s people, platforms and capabilities.Complementing these visits, INS Garuda will organise a Military Photo Exhibition at Forum Mall, Kochi, from Nov 20 to 22. It will feature photographs captured by naval photographers and journalists from across the country.The centrepiece of this year’s Navy Day celebrations will be the Naval Operations Demonstration at Ernakulam Wharf, Kochi, on the evening of Dec 3. The demonstration will bring alive Indian Navy’s combat readiness and operational prowess through coordinated displays by naval ships of Southern Naval Command, air assets and elite marine commandos, showcasing the synergy, precision and capabilities that underpin naval operations. Adding to the spectacle will be a hornpipe dance by the Sea Cadet Corps, a continuity drill and a special drone show.The celebrations will continue on Navy Day with a special musical concert and philharmonic orchestra performance by Southern Naval Command Band at Naval Base, Kochi, for a restricted audience.Navy Day, observed on Dec 4 every year, commemorates Indian Navy’s daring missile boat attacks on Karachi Harbour during the 1971 Indo-Pak War. articles.title: United by tehzeeb: How migrants became Lakhnavis
articles.summary: Lucknow’s migrant communities—Kashmiri, Parsi, Marathi, Gujarati, Bengali, Sikh and more—trace their roots, festivals and roles in shaping the city’s tehzeeb.
articles.body: In the lanes of Chowk, the old neighbourhoods of Aminabad, the academic corridors of Lucknow University, the railway settlements of Alambagh and Charbagh, and the newer colonies of Gomti Nagar and Indira Nagar, Lucknow’s composite culture continues to live through communities that came from faraway regions and made the city their own.Kashmiris, Parsis, Maharashtrians, Gujaratis, Bengalis, Sikhs, Odias, Anglo-Indians, Kayasthas, Malayalis, Sindhis and Uttarakhandis have all added distinct shades to the city’s cultural canvas. Some arrived in the courts of nawabs, some came with the railways and the colonial administration, some as refugees after Partition, and others in search of education, employment, trade and a life of dignity. Over generations, they became part of Lucknow’s tehzeeb, absorbing its nazakat and nafasat while keeping alive their own festivals, food, language, rituals and associations.They were not born Lakhnavis, but the city’s mannerisms, poise and warmth gave them a sense of belonging. In return, they enriched the city’s social, cultural, administrative, commercial and educational life.KashmirisThe Kashmiri community’s presence in Lucknow dates back to 1775, during the reign of Nawab Asaf-ud-Daula. Drawn by opportunities in the nawab’s court, many Kashmiris, well-versed in Persian, the official language of the time, secured important administrative and cultural positions. Their command over language and courtly etiquette helped them find a respected place in Awadh’s power structure.According to Ravi Kachru, secretary of Panun Kashmir, one of the earliest Kashmiri families to settle in Lucknow was the Sharga family, which made Rani Katra in Chowk its home. “Their arrival marked the beginning of a deep-rooted cultural connection between Kashmir and Awadh,” said Kachru.Over time, Kashmiri families became an integral part of Lucknow’s socio-cultural life. Many served in the royal court and held positions of trust and honour. Their homes carried memories of Kashmir, but their public lives became deeply intertwined with Awadhi customs, language and courtly refinement.Jyoti Kaul, president of the Kashmir Association, said, “Many Kashmiri families served in the royal court and held respectable positions, but over time, they gradually gave up their native language, assimilating linguistically and culturally into the Awadhi milieu. Despite this, their legacy remains embedded in the city’s rich historical tapestry.”ParsisThe Parsi community in Lucknow has always been small in number, but its historical importance has been significant. Nawrojee Damkawala is believed to have been the first Parsi to come to Lucknow between 1837 and 1842, during the reign of King Mohammad Ali Shah. He traded in silk and pearls from China with the nawabs and soon developed a close association with the city.He encouraged other Parsis to settle here, helping lay the foundation of a small but respected community. His son, Heerji Bhoi Nawrojee, later started the business of making horse-drawn carriages, an enterprise that became associated with the city’s elite lifestyle.Zarine Viccajee, Damkawala’s great-great-granddaughter, said the community adapted to local circumstances while preserving its identity.Today, around 45 Parsis remain in Lucknow. They celebrate festivals such as Navroz and Khordad Saal and continue to cherish their heritage through community gatherings, family traditions and collective memory.MaharashtriansThe Maharashtrian community, now numbering around 5,000 in Lucknow, traces its roots to the early 19th century after the exile of Bajirao II to Bithoor following the Third Anglo-Maratha War in 1818. Many Maharashtrians later joined royal courts across Uttar Pradesh, bringing with them administrative, military and cultural traditions.A second wave arrived in the early 20th century. Among them was Dr Laxman Gangadhar Natu, who came to Lucknow for medical practice and also pursued his passion for music. The families of Dr Natu, Maharane, Joshi and Vaishampaiyan were among the early Maharashtrian families that settled in the city.Dinesh Joshi, general secretary of Maharashtra Samaj, said Maharashtrians came to Lucknow in the early 1900s. “In 1921, the first Ganesh Puja began, and among the first families that came here were the families of Dr Natu, Maharane, Joshi and Vaishampaiyan,” he said.“My great-grandfather believed Lucknow offered the perfect blend of culture and opportunity,” said Anant Jayant Natu.With the establishment of Maharashtra Samaj in 1921, the community found a cultural anchor.“In 1971, my father Ankush Gadge encouraged people from Sangli and Satara to settle and start businesses in Lucknow. The community mainly resides in Aminabad, Gomti Nagar, Indira Nagar and Chowk,” said Umesh Patil, president of Marathi Samaj.GujaratisThe Gujarati community’s roots in Lucknow go back to the Nawabi era, particularly the reign of Nawab Asaf-ud-Daula in the late 18th century. Drawn by trade opportunities in textiles, gems and banking, Gujaratis arrived from cities such as Surat, Ahmedabad and Bhavnagar.They soon became trusted merchants and financiers to the royal court. Their reputation for business acumen, integrity and financial skill helped them establish a strong presence in the city’s commercial life.“Our ancestors were invited by the nawabs for their business acumen and integrity. They supplied fine fabrics, managed accounts and even advised on trade,” said Beena Shah, a senior member of the Gujarati community in Lucknow.BengalisThe Bengali community first came to Lucknow during the reign of Nawab Nasir-ud-din-Haider Shah between 1827 and 1837. Scholars such as Kalicharan Chattopadhyaya and Madhav Das were invited to oversee the Tara Wali Kothi observatory. Their arrival laid the foundation for one of the city’s most vibrant cultural communities.Bengalis introduced Durga Puja and Kali Puja to Lucknow. Over time, these festivals became iconic parts of the city’s cultural calendar.Enakshi Sinha, general secretary of Bengali Club, said the scholars were invited by the nawab to take care of Tara Wali Kothi. Later, their families and friends also travelled to Lucknow. They settled in areas such as Sundarbagh, Nazarbagh and Hewett Road, and later spread to Ashiyana, Aliganj and Daliganj.Institutions such as Bangiyo Yuvak Samiti, established in 1892, and Bengali Club, established in 1901, became major cultural pillars. Atul Krishna Sinha gifted land to the Bengali Club in 1914, strengthening the institutional base of the community.Today, around 2.5 lakh Bengalis live in Lucknow, including areas such as Model House and Ravindrapalli.SikhsLucknow’s Sikh community has strong roots in the Ramgarhia Biradari, known for carpentry, craftsmanship and railway wagon-making. Singar Singh, one of the pioneers, gave his name to Singar Nagar, a locality that still carries the memory of the community’s early presence.During Partition, many Sikhs arrived in Lucknow as refugees. People such as Kartar Singh Akali and Khadak Singh Akali rebuilt their lives in the city after displacement. Their stories became part of the larger narrative of courage, labour and resilience that marked post-Partition Lucknow.Today, around 80,000 Sikhs live in Lucknow, particularly in Charbagh, Alambagh, Rajendranagar and Guru Nanaknagar.Prominent members of the Sikh community include Trilochan Singh Chan, Narendra Singh Gulshan, Diwanaji and actor Amarjeet Singh.OdiasThe Odia community’s association with Lucknow began in 1946, when plumbers such as Raj Kishore Khuntia came to the city for work. Their arrival marked the beginning of a migration that would gradually grow through education, government service, art and professional opportunities.A major figure in the community’s history was sculptor Padma Shri Shridhar Mahapatra, who was associated with Santiniketan and later joined Lucknow University as a professor. His presence gave the community cultural visibility and helped anchor Odias in the intellectual and artistic life of the city.Prof DR Sahu, secretary of Odia Samaj, Lucknow, said among the first arrivals was Prof Shridhar Mahapatra of Fine Arts. Odias mainly live in Indira Nagar, Gomti Nagar, Rajajipuram and Aliganj. The Odia Samaj was established in 1994 and became an important platform for cultural activities.With thousands of members, the Odia community celebrates festivals and maintains social networks through Odia Samaj. According to Prof Sahu, around 36,000 Odia families now reside in Lucknow.Anglo-IndiansThe Anglo-Indian community grew during colonial times, when British officers settled in Lucknow with Indian families. Over time, the community became closely associated with education, music, administration, railways and public life.Their schools became enduring landmarks of excellence. Institutions such as La Martiniere, Loreto Convent and St Francis continue to hold a special place in the city’s educational landscape.Today, about 2,000 members of the community live in areas such as Lawrence Terrace and trans-Gomti. The Anglo-Indian Association, established in 1943, remains an important community body. Christmas and Easter continue to be celebrated with warmth, music, prayer and family gatherings.Prominent members of the community include Vir Chakra awardees Trevor and Denzil Keelor, educationist Peter Fanthome, civil servant Terrence Barker, musician George Figg and Dorothy Crosswaite, trustee of Uttar Pradesh’s only Anglo-Indian old-age home.KayasthasThe Kayastha community has had a deep and lasting influence on Lucknow’s administrative and cultural life. Its prominence dates back to the Nawabi era, when Persian was the language of the court. Fluent in Persian and skilled in documentation, accounts and correspondence, Kayasthas served as scribes, accountants, ministers and custodians of official records in the Nawabi bureaucracy.“Our ancestors were the cornerstone of the Nawabi administration. They kept records, managed finances and handled correspondence at the highest level,” said Anup Srivastava, a member of the community.Kayasthas settled in areas such as Lalbagh, Aminabad, Hazratganj and Saadatganj.MalayalisMalayalis began migrating to Lucknow in the 1950s for education, medicine and employment. Kerala Samajam, formed in 1956, became their cultural hub. Its first meeting was held at Krishna Cafe in Hazratganj under the leadership of Sanskrit scholar Prof Subramanian Iyer.The community gradually built schools, temples and cultural institutions while maintaining its links with Kerala. The Lord Ayyappa Mandir became one of its important religious centres. Festivals such as Onam, Christmas and cultural events like Kala Mela bring Malayalis together across generations.Jenson James, general secretary of Kerala Samajam, said nearly 5,000 Malayalis call Lucknow home. The community is spread across Gomti Nagar and other parts of the city.SindhisThe Sindhi community’s modern story in Lucknow began with Partition, when many families fled Sindh and arrived with little more than courage and determination. They rebuilt their lives through hard work, trade and mutual support.Refugees such as Satish Athwani started from scratch, selling ice balls and soaps to sustain their families. Pioneers such as Seth Motiram had already set up businesses, including Indira Tiles, and helped newcomers with food, education and basic support.The Lucknow Sindhu Samaj, established in 1955, became a major anchor for the community.Today, around 60,000 Sindhis live in Lucknow, said Murlidhar Ahuja, a member of the Sindhi community. Over the decades, they have become known for entrepreneurship, philanthropy and strong community networks.UttarakhandisMigrants from Uttarakhand began arriving in Lucknow in 1938 for jobs and studies. To support them, they formed Kumaon Parishad, which later became an important cultural and social body. In 2014, it merged into Uttarakhand Mahaparishad, which now serves as the community’s voice in the city.With around 4.5 lakh people, Uttarakhandis are one of Lucknow’s largest migrant groups. They celebrate Harela, Bakhai, Uttarakhand Mahotsav and Ramlila, keeping alive the traditions of the hills while being fully woven into the life of the city.Bharat Singh Bisht, general secretary of Uttarakhand Mahaparishad, said the community continues to maintain its cultural roots through festivals, associations and collective celebrations.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Lucknow | Silver Rate in Lucknow | Bank Holidays in Lucknow | Public Holidays in Lucknow | Lucknow AQI | Weather in Lucknow | Petrol Price in Lucknow | Diesel Price in Lucknow | CNG Price in Lucknow | LPG Price in LucknowStay updated with the latest Lucknow news. In the main event of the before the bell action, David Picasso of Colima, Mexico and Carl "Wonder Boy" Martin of the Philippines battled from bell to bell in a close, competitive fight with two different styles clashing.

In an upset, Martin (29-0, 21 KOs) won the biggest fight of his life over Picasso (33-2-1, 18 KOs) in a narrow split decision, 96-93 and 95-94 for Martin.

Martin and his team were emotional hearing the scores in their favor. After fighting for the first eight years of his career in the Philippines, Martin made his way to the U.S. and is now getting the opportunities he always dreamed about.

"I learned a lot in the U.S. I trained so much. I found so much good sparring. I won, I won, the WBC Silver title!" said Martin.

It is a difficult loss for Picasso against an opponent he was expected to look good against in a new weight division.

Martin came out with guns blazing. Picasso didn't appear entirely prepared for the activity and started the fight going backward. It wasn't where he wanted to be. Picasso couldn't get his jabs in gear to stop Martin from coming in.

In the third round, Martin threw a straight left down the middle, breaking Picasso's nose. Cutman Stitch Duran had his hands full but managed to keep the worst of the damage at bay to keep Picasso in the fight.

Picasso has experience on bigger stages, with his only previous loss coming to Naoya Inoue. He settled down in the second half of the fight and found more success landing body punches, slowing Martin down.

Martin's corner worked to try and keep him loose and relaxed. "You're having a lot of fun. Don't get careless. Be smart! Make him miss, make him pay!"

In the seventh round, Picasso turned the tables with a knockdown. Martin complained that Picasso had stepped on his foot, but a replay showed Picasso caught him with a clean punch. Picasso gained ground, winning the later rounds. Going into the tenth, both fighters and their corner knew the tenth round might make the difference. Martin won that tenth round, neutralizing the knockdown and taking the win.

Martin said he offered Picasso a rematch, who said he'd be up for it.

Team Mexico or Team Kazakh? Bek Murmaganget Claims KO for Both

The world has another charming heavy-handed puncher out of Kazakhstan to keep an eye on. Bek Nurmaganbet of Kazakhstan (17-0, 15 KOs) blew out Marcos Vazquez Rodriguez of Tijuana, Mexico (21-4-1, 10 KOs) in one vicious round, the highlight of the early session.

"I'm Team Mexico, but I'm Kazakh," smiled Nurmaganbet after his win. He said the knockout wasn't in his original game plan. "My plan was to start boxing, not knockout. But this is boxing. One punch changed my decision," said Nurmaganbet. It was his 13 th straight knockout win in his first fight scheduled for ten rounds.

Rodriguez was able to get up and leave the ring under his own power to the relief of Nurmaganbet who held off any celebration due to his concern about Rodriguez.

Nurmaganbet has been brought along quietly, appearing on deep undercards in support of champions like Canelo Alvarez and Stephen Fulton, but also quietly getting experience on regional cards around the world. You might not have noticed him before, but it's time to start paying attention.

"Of course I want the big fights," said Nurmaganbet. "I'm right now IBF ranking nine. IBF champion, Iglesias Cuban guy. I want this fight. I want to say to him, save my belt, I'm coming for you!" said Nurmaganbet in improving English. "Viva Mexico, Viva Kazakhstan!"

Nurmaganbet will inevitably be compared to his countryman Gennadiy Golovkin, and there's plenty of Triple G in him to like. The 28-year-old southpaw has a longer reach, and he uses it well.

Lightweight Sultan "El Nino" Al-Mohammed of Riyadh, Saudi Arabia (6-0, 4 KOs) thrilled his local fans with a power punching clinic over durable Erick Villegas of Mexico (5-3-3, 1 KO). In his first-round fight, Al-Mohammed wins by decision with scores 60-54, 59-55, 59-55.

"This is just the beginning. I will continue to be better and to be a world champion one day," said the 18-year-old talent from Syria. "I feel good, I feel so proud to be here."

Now trained by Eddy Reynoso after starting his career with Abel Sanchez, the "Mexican Style" approach was on display with heavy handed power jabs and impressive body shots. He is cutting off the ring well and putting on pressure nicely at this early stage.

Villegas had only been stopped once and wasn't afraid to stand and trade with Al-Mohammed, even if it wasn't the best idea. His legs, toughness, and a solid chin prevented Al-Mohammed from getting the knockout he wanted, but the rounds of work will be more valuable in the long run for Al-Mohammed. He's a work in progress and making progress.

Emiliano Rojo Vazquez of Mexico (23-0, 9 KOs) scored Mexico's only undercard win in the "Mexico vs the World" event over Flavius Biea of Romania (24-4, 12 KOs) in their super middleweight bout. It took just one round to get the TKO win.

Vazquez had too much strength and firepower at 20 years old for the 37-year-old veteran Biea. After just one round of pounding, the referee stopped in just before the bell in the first round to prevent any more unnecessary damage to Biea.

Super middleweights Brayan Leon of Cuba (13-0, 9 KOs) and Hector Aguirre of Mexico (7-1, 3 KOs) opened the card with undefeated records to protect. Fans up early enough were treated to a fun all action fight between two heavy-handed opponents.

It was Leon's power and precision versus Aguirre's volume punching and pressure. In a close fight, Leon prevailed on the scorecards. Two cards read 78-74, but the third card of 77-75 was much more representative of this close contest. Leon is trained by Eddy Reynoso, and he is adapting his style well to maximize his power.
